purpose: State-specific US overlays so Common Core is not presented as a single nationwide curriculum.

US_CA.label: California
US_CA.rule: Use content standards for grade requirements and the 2023 framework for implementation guidance.

US_TX.label: Texas
US_TX.rule: Use TEKS §111 grade-level expectations; Texas is not a Common Core state layer.

placement.summary: Three-digit place value through 1,000; California adds skip-counting by 100s to 2.NBT.2.
Compose, decompose, represent, compare and order whole numbers up to 1,200 and locate numbers on open number lines.
Extend place-value relationships through 100,000 and use number-line magnitude for rounding.

concepts.comparison_note: Texas Grade 2 extends the stated whole-number range to 1,200; California Grade 2 centres on numbers to 1,000.

placement.summary: Equal groups and rectangular arrays as foundations.
Interpret products/quotients, solve equal-group and array problems, use properties/inverse relationships and develop fact fluency within 100.
Model contextual multiplication as joining equal sets and division as separating into equal sets.

Use equal groups, arrays, area models, number-line jumps, skip counting, properties and inverse relationships; recall 10×10 facts and use strategies/algorithms including the standard algorithm for two-digit by one-digit multiplication.

concepts.comparison_note: Texas Grade 3 explicitly includes a standard-algorithm endpoint for two-digit by one-digit multiplication; California Grade 3 does not add that endpoint to its 3.OA cluster.

placement.summary: Fractions as numbers, number lines, simple equivalence and comparison; denominators 2,3,4,6,8.
Extend equivalence using visual fraction models.
Early fractional-unit ideas with halves, fourths and eighths using concrete models.
Fractional units, strip diagrams and number lines; represent/explain equivalent fractions with denominators 2,3,4,6,8.

concepts.comparison_note: Both formalise fraction-number reasoning in Grade 3; Texas explicitly places a concrete fractional-unit strand in Grade 2.

placement.summary: Area in square units; connect rectangle area to multiplication/addition and decompose rectilinear figures.
Cover rectangles with square units and count units to determine area.
Rectangle area through rows × unit squares and composite rectangular area by decomposition.

concepts.comparison_note: Texas explicitly starts square-unit area measurement in Grade 2; California's main area cluster is Grade 3.

placement.summary: Ratios, unit rates, equivalent-ratio tables, tape diagrams, double number lines, equations and percent as rate per 100.

Distinguish additive/multiplicative relationships; ratios, rates, percent, equivalent forms and unit rates using models, fractions/decimals, grids, strip diagrams, number lines, tables, graphs, proportions and scale factors.

concepts.comparison_note: Both place formal ratio/rate work in Grade 6; Texas explicitly integrates benchmark percents and fraction-decimal-percent equivalence in its proportionality strand.

placement.summary: Add within 1,000 using place-value-based strategies and algorithms; no single standard algorithm is required by this Grade 3 standard.
Fluently add multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
Use mental strategies and place-value-based algorithms for multi-digit addition/subtraction and solve problems within 1,000; the standard algorithm is not named here.
Solve addition/subtraction problems within 1,000 fluently using place value, operation properties and inverse relationships.
Add whole numbers and decimals to hundredths using the standard algorithm.

concepts.comparison_note: Both California and Texas make the standard addition algorithm explicit in Grade 4, while earlier grades retain broader strategy/algorithm language.

placement.summary: Subtract within 1,000 using place-value-based strategies and algorithms.
Fluently subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
Use mental strategies and place-value-based algorithms for multi-digit subtraction and solve within 1,000.
Solve addition/subtraction problems within 1,000 fluently through place-value and operation relationships.
Subtract whole numbers and decimals to hundredths using the standard algorithm.

concepts.comparison_note: The explicit standard subtraction algorithm endpoint is Grade 4 in both state standards in this comparison.

placement.summary: Multiply multi-digit whole numbers using place value and operation properties and explain with equations, arrays and/or area models; the standard algorithm is not required by this Grade 4 standard.
Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
Use strategies and algorithms, including the standard algorithm, for two-digit by one-digit multiplication; strategies may include mental math, partial products and operation properties.

Represent two-digit by two-digit products with arrays/area models/equations and use strategies and algorithms, including the standard algorithm, for up to four-digit by one-digit and two-digit by two-digit multiplication.
Multiply a three-digit number by a two-digit number fluently using the standard algorithm.

concepts.comparison_note: Texas explicitly names the standard multiplication algorithm from Grade 3 for a narrower calculation type; California makes the standard multi-digit multiplication algorithm a Grade 5 fluency requirement.

placement.summary: Find quotients/remainders up to four-digit by one-digit using place-value/property strategies and explain with equations, arrays and/or area models.
Extend to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors using strategies and equations/arrays/area models; no standard algorithm is required by this Grade 5 standard.
Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.
Determine quotients using the relationship between multiplication and division; no standard written-division algorithm is named.
Represent up to four-digit by one-digit division with arrays/area models/equations and use strategies and algorithms, including the standard algorithm.
Solve up to four-digit by two-digit whole-number division proficiently using strategies and the standard algorithm.

concepts.comparison_note: Texas makes standard whole-number division explicit in Grade 4 for one-digit divisors and extends it in Grade 5; California keeps model/strategy-based division through Grade 5 and makes the standard multi-digit division algorithm explicit in Grade 6.

state_comparison_rules: Show Common Core as a baseline only when no state is selected.
When California or Texas is selected, use the state requirement as the curriculum layer.
Keep California framework guidance separate from California content standards.
Never generalise Texas sequencing to the rest of the US.
Show state differences in range, representation and algorithm timing rather than normalising them away.
